title: Letters that stand for numbers
objectives: Read a letter as a number we do not know yet
Write an expression for a quantity described in words
Substitute a value into an expression, multiplying before adding

screens.prose: Each sealed envelope holds the same amount, in £1 coins. You cannot see inside. A tray holds 3 envelopes and 4 loose £1 coins.

state.caption: Each ? is a sealed envelope. Every envelope holds the same amount.

screens.question: You learn that each envelope holds £5. How much money is on the tray?

hints.text: Work out the envelopes first, then the loose coins.
Three envelopes, each with £5 inside.
Three envelopes of £5 make £15. Add the 4 loose coins.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count £5 for each envelope, then add the loose coins.

byKey.added: You added the number of envelopes to the amount in one. Three envelopes of £5 make 3 × 5, not 3 + 5.
byKey.all-envelopes: You counted the loose coins as envelopes too. Only 3 envelopes hold £5; the 4 coins are £1 each.
byKey.coins-inside: You put the 4 loose coins inside every envelope. They sit on the tray once, so they add £4 once.
byKey.one-envelope: You counted one envelope. The tray holds three of them.

explain.text: You multiplied for the envelopes and added for the loose coins: $3 \times 5 + 4 = 19$. If each envelope held £6, only the first part would change. The 4 loose pounds stay put.

screens.prose: Same tray: 3 envelopes and 4 loose £1 coins. Someone refills every envelope so that each now holds £6.
screens.question: Drag the point to the money on the tray now.

hints.text: Do the same two steps as before, with £6 in each envelope.
Three envelopes of £6 come first.
$3 \times 6 = 18$, then add the 4 loose coins.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply for the envelopes, then add the loose coins.

byKey.added: You added 3, 6 and 4. Three envelopes of £6 make 3 × 6.
byKey.one-envelope: You counted one envelope. There are three.
byKey.coins-inside: You put the loose coins into each envelope. They are on the tray once.
byKey.old: That is the total with £5 in each envelope. Each now holds £6.

explain.text: You did the same two steps with a new amount: $3 \times 6 + 4 = 22$. Only the amount in an envelope changed. The steps did not.

screens.prose: Call the amount in one envelope $n$ pounds. The letter stands for a number we do not know yet. Three envelopes hold $3 \times n$, written $3n$. So the first tray held $3n + 4$ pounds.
screens.question: Which expression gives the money on this tray?

options.why: You counted the loose coins as envelopes. Only the 2 envelopes hold $n$ each; the 5 coins are £1 each.
You swapped the numbers. The 2 goes with the envelopes, so it multiplies $n$.
You counted the 2 envelopes as £2. Each envelope holds $n$, so two hold $2n$.

hints.text: How many envelopes, and how many loose coins?
Two envelopes, each holding $n$.
Two envelopes hold $2n$. The 5 loose coins add 5.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply $n$ by the number of envelopes, then add the loose coins.

explain.text: Two envelopes hold $2 \times n = 2n$, and the loose coins add 5. So the tray holds $2n + 5$ pounds, whatever $n$ turns out to be. A combination of numbers and letters like this is an **expression**.

screens.prose: Now no envelopes, just words. A broker charges a £3 fee on every order, plus £2 for each share you buy. You buy $n$ shares in one order.

state.caption: £3 once, then £2 for each of the $n$ shares

screens.question: Write the cost of the order in pounds.

hints.text: Which part is paid once, and which part is paid per share?
The fee box is paid once. The £2 box is paid $n$ times.
Once: 3. Per share: $2 \times n = 2n$. Add them.

feedback.correct: A £3 fee once, and £2 for each of $n$ shares.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the one-off fee to £2 times the number of shares.

byKey.fee-each: You charged the fee on every share. The £3 is paid once per order, so it is added, not multiplied.
byKey.swapped: You swapped the numbers. The £2 is the per-share charge, so it multiplies $n$.
byKey.added-once: You added the £2 once. It is paid for each share, so it is $2 \times n$.

explain.text: The fee is paid once, so it is added: 3. The share charge is paid $n$ times, so it multiplies: $2n$. The cost is $3 + 2n$ pounds, and $2n + 3$ means the same.

screens.prose: To use $3 + 2n$, put a number in for $n$. This is **substituting**. The table shows the cost for some order sizes.
screens.question: What does an order of 50 shares cost?

hints.text: Look at how the rows for 1 and 10 shares were worked out.
The middle column is $2n$: two times the shares.
$2 \times 50 = 100$, then add the £3 fee.

feedback.correct: £100 for the shares and £3 for the fee.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out $2 \times 50$ first, then add 3.

byKey.side-by-side: You wrote 2 next to 50 to get 250. $2n$ means $2 \times n$, so it is 100.
byKey.plus-first: You added 3 and 2 first, then multiplied by 50. That charges the fee on every share.
byKey.added: You added 3, 2 and 50. The 2 multiplies the 50.

explain.text: You put 50 in place of $n$: $2 \times 50 = 100$, then $3 + 100 = 103$. The order is £103. The same expression gives every row of the table.

screens.prose: Every block marked $n$ weighs the same unknown amount. The left pan holds $2n + 4$. The right pan holds $3n$. When $n = 3$, the left pan is heavier, as shown.

state.caption: With $n = 3$: 10 on the left, 9 on the right

screens.question: Which pan is heavier when $n = 5$?

options.why: You assumed the heavier pan stays heavier. Substitute $n = 5$: the left is $2 \times 5 + 4 = 14$, the right is 15.
You may have tried $n = 4$, where both pans weigh 12. At $n = 5$ the right pan has 15 and the left 14.

hints.text: Put 5 in for every $n$ on both pans.
The left pan is $2n + 4$.
Left: $2 \times 5 + 4 = 14$. Right: $3 \times 5 = 15$.

feedback.correct: 15 beats 14, so the right pan goes down.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Substitute $n = 5$ into each pan and compare.

explain.text: With $n = 5$ the left pan weighs 14 and the right pan 15. Which pan wins depends on $n$. At $n = 4$ both weigh 12, the one value that balances the scale.

canvas.caption: With $n = 5$: 14 on the left, 15 on the right

screens.prose: Back to the broker: an order of $n$ shares costs $3 + 2n$ pounds. Ravi prices an order of 4 shares. He works left to right: $3 + 2 = 5$, then $5 \times 4 = 20$.

state.caption: £3 once, then £2 for each of the 4 shares

screens.question: What does an order of 4 shares really cost?

options.why: That is Ravi's answer. Adding 3 and 2 first charges the £3 fee on every share.
You read $2n$ as 24, the digits side by side. $2n$ means $2 \times 4 = 8$.
You added 3, 2 and 4. The £2 is paid for each share, so it multiplies the 4.

hints.text: In $3 + 2n$, which two things are stuck together?
The fee box is paid once, whatever the order size.
$2n$ means $2 \times 4 = 8$. Then add the £3 fee once.

feedback.correct: £8 for the shares, plus the £3 fee once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out $2n$ first, then add the 3.

byKey.plus-first: You followed Ravi. Adding first turns $3 + 2n$ into $5n$, which charges £5 per share. The fee is paid once.

explain.text: $2n$ is a product, so it is worked out before the adding: $3 + 2 \times 4 = 3 + 8 = 11$. Ravi's order gives $5n$, a different expression. At 4 shares it overcharges by £9.

screens.prose: Each time, the letter stood for one number, and a number written against the letter meant multiply: $$2n = 2 \times n \qquad 3 + 2n = 3 + (2 \times n)$$ Substitute by putting the number in for the letter. Multiply before you add.
screens.question: What is $5n$ when $n = 7$?

options.why: You wrote 5 and 7 side by side. $5n$ means $5 \times n$.
You added 5 and 7. A number against a letter means multiply.

hints.text: What sign is hiding between the 5 and the $n$?
$5n = 5 \times n = 5 \times 7$.

explain.text: $5n$ is $5 \times n$, so with $n = 7$ it is 35. The hidden sign is always a multiplication.

screens.prose: A gym charges a £25 joining fee, then £12 for every month you stay a member.
screens.question: Write the total paid, in pounds, after $m$ months.

hints.text: Which charge is paid once, and which is paid every month?
The £25 is paid once, like the broker's fee.
Once: 25. Every month: $12 \times m = 12m$. Add them.

feedback.correct: £25 once, then £12 for each of the $m$ months.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the one-off fee to £12 times the number of months.

byKey.fee-monthly: You charged the joining fee every month. It is paid once, so it is added, not multiplied by $m$.
byKey.swapped: You swapped the numbers. The £12 is the monthly charge, so it multiplies $m$.

explain.text: A one-off amount is added and a per-month amount multiplies the letter: $25 + 12m$. Check with $m = 1$: £37 after one month, which matches £25 plus £12.

screens.prose: A broker charges £1.50 per trade plus 2p for every share in the trade. The table shows the commission on three trades.
screens.question: Which expression gives the commission, in pounds, on a trade of $n$ shares?

options.why: You used 2 for 2p. In pounds 2p is 0.02, otherwise 100 shares would cost £201.50.
You added the fee to the per-share charge, so the fee is paid on every share. 100 shares would cost £152.
You swapped the two charges. Then 100 shares would cost £150.02, not £3.50.

hints.text: Which charge is paid once per trade, and which per share?
Test an option on the first row: 100 shares cost £3.50.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write 2p in pounds, then test your choice on a row of the table.

explain.text: The £1.50 is paid once per trade and 2p is £0.02 per share: $1.50 + 0.02n$. For 2,000 shares that is $1.50 + 40 = 41.50$, matching the table. Testing a row is a quick way to catch a wrong expression.

ideas: A letter stands for a number we do not know yet. The same letter is the same number everywhere it appears.
A number written against a letter means multiply: $2n = 2 \times n$. A one-off amount is added; a per-item amount multiplies the letter.
To substitute, put the number in for the letter, multiply first, then add.

formula.name: Fee plus a charge per item
formula.note: The 3 is paid once. The 2 is paid for each of the $n$ items.

summary.trap: $3 + 2n$ is not $5n$. Work out $2n$ first, then add the 3.

quiz.prose: Cinema tickets cost £9 each. Every order also pays a £2 booking fee.
quiz.question: Which expression gives the cost, in pounds, of an order of $t$ tickets?

options.why: You charged the booking fee on every ticket. It is paid once per order.
You swapped the numbers. The £9 is per ticket, so it multiplies $t$.
You added the ticket price once. Each of the $t$ tickets costs £9.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the per-ticket price by $t$, then add the fee.

explain.text: The ticket price is paid $t$ times, so it is $9t$. The booking fee is paid once, so it is added: $9t + 2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out $3 \times 0$ first.

byKey.three: You treated $3n$ as 3. Three lots of 0 is 0.
byKey.side-by-side: You wrote 3 next to 0 to make 30. $3n$ means $3 \times 0$.
byKey.all-zero: You multiplied the whole expression by 0. Only the $3n$ part is multiplied; the 4 stays.

explain.text: $3n = 3 \times 0 = 0$, so $4 + 3n = 4 + 0 = 4$. A letter can stand for 0, and then its term vanishes.

quiz.prose: Your account holds $q$ shares priced at £12.40 each, and £150 in cash.
quiz.question: Write the value of the account in pounds.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the price by $q$, then add the cash.

byKey.cash-each: You added the cash to the share price, so the cash counts once per share. It is held once.
byKey.swapped: You swapped the numbers. The price, £12.40, is per share, so it multiplies $q$.

explain.text: The shares are worth price times quantity, $12.40q$. The cash is added once: $12.40q + 150$ pounds.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply first, then subtract.

byKey.side-by-side: You wrote 5 next to 6 to make 56. $5p$ means $5 \times 6 = 30$.
byKey.subtract-first: You worked out $5 - 4$ first. Multiplying comes before subtracting.
